title: Cleerly's PARAMOUNT trial — AI coronary-plaque analysis beats usual care
subtitle: The first randomized trial of AI-QCT-guided care met its primary 180-day composite endpoint with a win ratio of 2.00 against usual care, improved diagnostic certainty, and drove more patients to lipid-lowering therapy. Results were late-breaking at AHA 2026, not yet peer-reviewed.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Cleerly presented late-breaking results from the PARAMOUNT trial at the American Heart Association 2026 Scientific Sessions in Chicago on November 7. PARAMOUNT is a prospective, randomized, open-label trial comparing care guided by AI-based quantitative coronary CT (AI-QCT) with usual care in patients with suspected coronary artery disease. On a prespecified hierarchical composite at 180 days, plaque-based care was favored over usual care with a win ratio of 2.00, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.56, p<0.0001 — a strongly positive primary endpoint. The AI-guided arm also showed higher diagnostic certainty and higher initiation of lipid-lowering therapy, with better LDL-C reductions. Among patients who underwent invasive coronary angiography, 38% in the AI-QCT-guided arm did not go on to revascularization with PCI or bypass surgery, compared with 60% in the usual-care arm. The data have not yet been peer-reviewed; full publication is expected in early 2027.

This is the first randomized trial of AI-enabled plaque-based care in cardiology to meet its primary endpoint, and it matters because the AI-guided arm did not merely match usual care — it changed the downstream treatment path. More patients on lipid-lowering therapy, better LDL-C control, and fewer unnecessary revascularizations after angiography are the kinds of outcome shifts that eventually move guidelines. Coronary CT with AI plaque quantification has been accumulating observational evidence for several years; a randomized positive primary endpoint is the kind of evidence payers and societies have been waiting for.

The caveats are the usual ones for a sponsor-led late-breaker — Cleerly is the maker of the AI tool, and the results are preliminary pending peer review. The mechanism, though, is grounded. AI-QCT does not replace the cardiologist; it quantifies plaque characteristics (burden, composition, remodeling) that are hard to read by eye and feeds that information back into the care path. That fits the pattern where AI delivers the largest clinical value — not autonomous diagnosis, but structured measurement of things humans measure poorly or inconsistently, with a human still in the loop for the decision.

A takeaway for learners: when you hear about AI in medicine, watch for the trial design. The strongest evidence is a randomized trial with a hard outcome and a prespecified endpoint, published or presented at a major society meeting with discussion. Observational and retrospective studies can flatter a tool; a randomized trial constrains that. If you work in or around healthcare, the pattern worth studying is this one — a narrow quantification task, embedded in an existing clinical workflow, measured against outcomes that matter. That is where AI is earning its place in medicine right now.
